title: Out of the ashes
text: The Great Fire of London began in the small hours of 2 September 1666, in the bakery on Pudding Lane, and for three days it {{1}} through the wooden city unchecked. The damage was {{2}}: some 13,000 houses, 87 churches and the medieval cathedral of St Paul's were destroyed, and perhaps 100,000 people were left homeless. Remarkably, the death toll is thought to have been {{3}} small — the official count was six, though historians suspect the true figure was higher. The mayor's famous refusal to pull down houses, on the grounds that the fire would {{4}} out of its own accord, cost the city precious hours. What followed, however, {{5}} the disaster's place in history: rather than rebuild in wood, London rose in brick and stone, with wider streets, a rebuilding tax and, at its centre, Wren's new dome. The fire also {{6}} the last major outbreak of bubonic plague in England — the rats, their fleas and so many of the crowded houses that sheltered them had gone up in smoke. A monument still stands near where the fire began, its inscription {{7}} blaming Catholics, a paragraph not removed until 1830. Cities still study 1666, because the lesson has never {{8}}: flammable building stock in a dense city is a catastrophe waiting for a spark.

gaps.explanation: 'for three days it swept through the wooden city' — spread rapidly; wander, stroll and dawdle are aimless or slow movement.
'The damage was immense' — vast in scale; immersed = sunk in liquid, immaterial = irrelevant, immune = protected.
'thought to have been remarkably small' — surprisingly so; the sentence stresses surprise, which the other adverbs do not convey.
'the fire would burn out of its own accord' — 'burn out' = stop for lack of fuel; burst out = suddenly begin, which reverses the meaning.
'secured the disaster's place in history' — made it certain; secrete = hide, sequester = set apart, seclude = isolate.
'also marked the last major outbreak' — signalled its end; mask = conceal, mock = ridicule, mar = spoil.
'its inscription wrongly blaming Catholics' — unjustly, since the paragraph was factually false; the other adverbs do not convey error.
'the lesson has never dated' — never become out of date; 'date' here means age, a use the near-forms do not share.
